title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
hookLine: in the middle of the lament: God's mercies "are new every morning"

lines: A VOICE FROM THE BOTTOM OF A PIT.
THIS I RECALL TO MY MIND.
cards: Halfway through Lamentations, a man speaks from what feels like the bottom of a pit. He's been led into darkness, he says, hedged in so he can't get out, his prayers shut out. Line after line, it gets heavier.
Then, with no warning, one sentence changes direction: "This I recall to my mind, Therefore have I hope." Nothing outside him has changed. The city is still in ruins.
What changes is what he chooses to remember.

teach.b: New every morning. Here's what he recalls, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Surely the LORD's mercies are not consumed, Surely His compassions fail not. They are new every morning; Great is Thy faithfulness."
Two words carry the weight. Mercies, in Hebrew chasadim: steady, loyal kindness, the kind that keeps a promise. Compassions, rachamim: tenderness, the way a parent feels toward a child.
Those, he says, don't run out.

They aren't stored up once, like grain in a barn, to be rationed until they're gone. They arrive fresh, a little like the manna in the wilderness, which came each morning and couldn't be saved for later.
Then he adds: "The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; Therefore will I hope in Him." Now notice where this sits. Not at the end of the book, as a happy ending.
Right in the middle. The chapters before it mourn; the chapters after it mourn again.

teach.h: HOPE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE LAMENT.
teach.b: The hope doesn't erase the lament; the lament surrounds it on both sides. It's an honest shape for hope: not a door out of sorrow, but a lamp lit inside it. And the claim is small and daily.
Not, everything is fine. Just: this morning, something was given that wasn't there last night. The phrase has traveled into the start of the Jewish day.

teach.h: GREAT IS THY FAITHFULNESS, AT DAWN.
teach.b: Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, thanks God for returning the soul, and ends with these words: rabbah emunatecha, great is your faithfulness. A line from the ruins, said at dawn.

how: Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, thanks God for returning the soul and ends with the words of Lamentations 3:23, 'great is your faithfulness.'

o: the short thank-you prayer said on waking
the night prayer said just before sleep
the blessing said over bread at meals

games.q: new every morning — tap the pairs.

s: Lamentations is grief from start to finish, with no hope in it
in its middle: 'they are new every morning; great is Thy faithfulness.'
the hope comes at the very end, as a happy ending
it sits in the middle, with mourning before it and after it.
Modeh Ani, said on waking, borrows 'great is your faithfulness' from Lamentations
rabbah emunatecha: the same words, said at dawn.

games.q: you're the voice in Lamentations, at the bottom of the pit. nothing outside has changed. what do you do?
o: call one thing to mind, and hope.
games.why: 'this I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.' the hope begins with a memory, not a rescue.

practice: Go back over the hours since you woke and find one thing given to you today that you didn't earn or plan: light through a window, a kind word, a body that got out of bed, a cup of something warm.
Hold that one thing for a moment, the way the voice in the pit held one memory. If you pray, you can say the old words: great is thy faithfulness.

wordCard.voice: Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, which thanks God for a new day and ends with Lamentations' words: great is your faithfulness. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew of Lamentations 3:23: new for the mornings.

carryVoice: Your line: a lamp lit inside it. Hope, right in the middle of the lament. Until tomorrow.
